item.title: AlphaProof Code verified Signal's protocol code with 6.5 million lines of Lean in four weeks: what AI-written proofs mean for the software you depend on
item.description: DeepMind's five-person team used agents on Gemini 4 Carbon and Claude Opus 5.5 to prove security properties of libsignal at the machine-code level; the trusted part is the 26,000 lines of spec, and that is where review now belongs.
item.content:encoded:
DeepMind's five-person team used agents on Gemini 4 Carbon and Claude Opus 5.5 to prove security properties of libsignal at the machine-code level; the trusted part is the 26,000 lines of spec, and that is where review now belongs.

Google DeepMind published AlphaProof Code on November 10, a system in which human experts and AI agents together produce machine-checked proofs that software meets a formal specification. Its first target was libsignal, the reference implementation of the Signal protocol that also underpins encryption in WhatsApp and Google Messages. The team proved forward secrecy, post-compromise security and authentication for the post-quantum PQXDH handshake and the Triple Ratchet, for libsignal version 0.105.4 and the spqr library at 1.6.0, and it proved them about the compiled AArch64 machine code rather than the protocol design.

How it worked

Five researchers spent four weeks. Humans and agents running on Gemini 4 Carbon and Claude Opus 5.5 wrote the specifications, the statements of what had to be true, and the semantics of the instructions and system calls involved: about 26,000 lines in total, covering 467 instructions and 31 system calls. Agents on Carbon then generated roughly 6.5 million lines of Lean proofs. Lean, the proof assistant, rejects any proof that does not follow, so the volume of generated text is checked mechanically rather than read. To show the method catches real flaws, the team re-inserted two historical, already-patched libsignal bugs and demonstrated that the security theorems fail on each build. The specifications and proofs are being released under Apache 2.0 in a public repository; a full rebuild reportedly needs between 15 and 34 GiB of memory.

For comparison, the seL4 microkernel's verification took about twenty person-years and CompCert's verified compiler about six. Signal's chief technology officer, Ehren Kret, said the work gives Signal greater confidence in its code's privacy guarantees.

What it does not cover

DeepMind is specific about the limits. The proofs apply to its own build of libsignal, run through a small command-line wrapper, not to the Signal, WhatsApp or Google Messages applications. Side channels, such as timing, are out of scope for parts of the analysis. Trust-on-first-use behaviour was not exercised. There is no quantum security guarantee, only the classical properties, and the proofs carry a vacuity bound after roughly 25,000 messages in a session. None of those is a flaw in the result; each is a reminder that a proof is only as broad as its statement.

Why this matters for developers

Formal verification has been the gold standard for safety-critical code and almost nobody has used it, because the specification and proof effort cost more than the software. If agents can do the proof-writing at this scale, the cost moves to the specification: deciding, precisely, what the code must guarantee. That is a smaller job, but it is the one that requires judgment, and it is where errors become invisible. A proof that your code satisfies the wrong spec is worth nothing, and Lean cannot tell you the spec is wrong. The practical change is that review effort for critical libraries should move from reading implementations to reading and arguing about specifications, and that "is there a machine-checked spec for this" becomes a reasonable question to ask a vendor.

It also matters that the agents ran on two vendors' models. Google reported the result on the day it opened Gemini 4 Carbon to all paying developers, and the Carbon-for-cyber variant leads Google's patching benchmark; the implication is that proof generation is a product category, not a one-off.

The counter-argument

This is a Google research result announced alongside a Google model launch, using a target that Signal cooperated on. Nobody outside DeepMind has yet rebuilt the proofs. Proof volume is not a measure of assurance; 6.5 million lines says the agents were prolific, not that the 26,000-line spec is right, and the two re-injected bugs were chosen by the team. Four weeks also followed years of groundwork in Lean, in instruction semantics and in prior verification research that the announcement compresses. The honest claim is narrower: for a well-understood protocol with a cooperative maintainer, AI reduced the proof effort by one to two orders of magnitude.

What to do

If you ship or depend on cryptographic libraries, read the released specification rather than the headline, and compare it with the properties your threat model actually needs. If you maintain a critical open-source library, consider publishing a formal statement of its guarantees now; the proof may follow sooner than you expect, and the spec is the part that needs your knowledge. For security teams, add verified-build status to the questions you ask of messaging, VPN and key-management vendors, and treat machine-code-level proofs as the standard to ask for, since design-level proofs leave the compiler and build pipeline out. And watch for reproductions: the repository is public, and the first independent rebuild will say more than the announcement.

item.title: Muse Ember at $0.10 and LongCat-2.5 under MIT: the budget tier is now where agent costs are decided
item.description: Meta's smallest model matches Claude Haiku 5.5 on the Artificial Analysis index at a third of the cost per task, and Meituan has handed developers a 1.6-trillion-parameter model to run themselves.
item.content:encoded:
Meta's smallest model matches Claude Haiku 5.5 on the Artificial Analysis index at a third of the cost per task, and Meituan has handed developers a 1.6-trillion-parameter model to run themselves.

Two releases this week moved the cheap end of the model market, which is where most agent tokens are actually spent. Meta launched Muse Ember, its smallest multimodal model, and Meituan published the full weights of LongCat-2.5 under the MIT licence.

Muse Ember

Ember is priced at $0.10 per million input tokens, $0.004 for cached input and $0.50 for output on prompts up to 200K tokens; above that, all three rates triple. It takes text, image, audio and video input, has a 1-million-token window, and is positioned explicitly for repeated agent sub-tasks: tool calls, routing, extraction, document summarisation and coding sub-steps. It is available through Meta's own model API and on Google Cloud Marketplace.

The list price matches Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna exactly. What differs is behaviour. Artificial Analysis, which tests models independently, scores Ember 36 on its Intelligence Index, level with Haiku 5.5, but measures its cost per task at $0.14 against Haiku's $0.41, because Ember emits roughly a third as many output tokens to reach the same answers. On the Coding Agent Index inside Meta's Muse Code harness it scores 46 against 37 for Claude Code with Haiku and 31 for Codex with GPT-6 Luna. Its weaknesses are also measurable: 27.2% on FrontierCode 2.0 against Haiku's 34.9%, and 21.1% accuracy on the AA-Omniscience knowledge test, where it declines to answer 64% of questions. For a model meant to sit inside a loop rather than talk to a user, declining is often the right behaviour.

LongCat-2.5

Meituan, the Chinese delivery company that has quietly become a serious model lab, released the LongCat-2.5 checkpoint on Hugging Face on November 9, a week after announcing the model. It is a mixture-of-experts design with about 1.6 trillion total parameters and roughly 48 billion active per token, with vision input, a hosted API at a limited-time $0.30 / $1.20, and serving optimisations including 4-bit expert weights on Chinese accelerators. Meituan's own figures put it at 88.4 on Terminal Bench v2.1, within a point of GPT-5.6 Sol and Claude Opus 5, and 64.6 on DeepSWE v1.1, up from 9.7 for LongCat-2.0.

The caveats are the usual ones for vendor tables: the closed baselines Meituan chose are a generation old, Terminal Bench v4.0 leaderboard scores for GPT-6.1 Sol and Opus 5.5 are far higher, and a 1.6T checkpoint is not something most teams will self-host. The licence is the news. MIT terms impose no usage restrictions, and unlike DeepSeek, which a Department of Homeland Security order excluded from federal civilian procurement in October, no US restriction currently names Meituan.

The counter-argument

Cheap tokens invite waste. A budget model that is three times cheaper per task but is called ten times more often inside a poorly designed agent loop costs more, not less, and Ember's 3x surcharge above 200K tokens punishes exactly the long-context agent patterns Meta is marketing it for. Open weights also shift cost rather than removing it: hosting LongCat-2.5 well needs multi-GPU nodes and operations skill that a $0.30 API rate makes hard to justify.

What to do

Instrument your agents to report cost per completed task, not tokens. Move the mechanical steps, routing, extraction, tool-call formatting and summarisation, to Ember or Haiku and keep the planning step on a mid-tier model. Cap context before the 200K cliff. If you are evaluating LongCat-2.5, test it through a hosted provider first and only consider self-hosting once you know the workload is stable. And re-read your vendor concentration policy: three different companies now anchor the three price tiers in our tracker.

item.title: OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol discount ends November 30. Here is the price ladder to move to
item.description: Two vendors' promotional rates expire within a day of each other. OpenAI's pricing page now shows four GPT-6 tiers from $0.10 to $10 per million tokens, and our tracker has caught up.
item.content:encoded:
Two vendors' promotional rates expire within a day of each other. OpenAI's pricing page now shows four GPT-6 tiers from $0.10 to $10 per million tokens, and our tracker has caught up.

OpenAI's API pricing page now carries a footnote developers should read before the end of the month: promotional pricing for GPT-5.6 Sol is available until November 30, 2026. Since August 21 the model has been billed at $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output, a cut from its $5 / $30 list rate that OpenAI announced as a three-month promotion. On December 1 the list rate returns, a 25% increase on input and 50% on output for anyone still on the model.

It lands a day after Google's launch pricing on Gemini 4 Argon ends, taking that model from $2 / $10 to $4 / $20. Two of the three largest API vendors are re-pricing within 24 hours of each other, which is a good moment to look at the whole ladder.

The ladder OpenAI actually wants you on

Our pricing tracker had been carrying GPT-5.6 Sol, Terra and Luna from secondary sources. Reading OpenAI's model pages directly today, we confirmed those rows and found four GPT-6-generation tiers that were not in the tracker at all. All carry a 1.05-million-token context window and 128K maximum output, and all double input rates and add 50% to output on requests over 272K input tokens.

GPT-6 Astra remains the top tier at $10 / $50, with cached input at $1. GPT-6.1 Sol, launched September 30, is $2 / $10 with cached input at $0.10, and OpenAI's own launch post says it is "getting close to Astra on complex work" at a fifth of the price, citing 75.2% on DeepSWE v1.1 against 68.8% for the older GPT-6 Sol and 71.4% on OSWorld 2.0 against Astra's 73.5%. GPT-6.1 Terra is $1 / $5 with cached input at $0.05, aimed at visual reasoning and computer use. GPT-6 Luna is $0.10 / $0.50, the volume tier. The older GPT-6 Sol stays at $2 / $10 but with cached input at $0.20, double the 6.1 rate.

Below that, GPT-5.6 Terra is $2 / $12 and GPT-5.6 Luna $0.20 / $1.20; GPT-5.4 mini is $0.75 / $4.50 and GPT-5.4 nano, now marked deprecated, $0.20 / $1.25. GPT-6 Cyber, the gated security model released November 5, is $20 / $100.

Read as a whole, the message is clear. A developer paying promotional rates on GPT-5.6 Sol is paying twice what GPT-6.1 Sol costs for a model OpenAI describes as less capable.

Where the real discounts are

Three modifiers matter more than list price for most workloads. Cached input on GPT-6.1 Sol is 5% of the input rate, so a long, stable system prompt or document is almost free on repeated calls. Batch and Flex processing are 50% off across the GPT-6 tiers. Fast mode costs 2x and the new Ultrafast mode on GPT-6.1 Sol costs 6x ($12 / $60).

OpenAI buys the Git layer under Codex

In the same week OpenAI agreed to acquire Pierre Computer Company, a San Francisco developer with a staff "barely in the double digits", for an undisclosed sum. Pierre built Code.Storage, an infrastructure layer for Git, and the open-source Trees and Diffs libraries that Codex already uses for rendering and reviewing changes. OpenAI says Code.Storage will be folded into Codex, existing customers can keep using it until then, and the open-source projects stay open. The deal follows OpenAI's description earlier that week of Pando, a new Git back end designed for many humans and agents committing to the same repository in parallel. Owning the storage layer under the code its agents write is the logical next step for a company that wants Codex to be the place work happens rather than a tool that visits it.

What to do

Export October usage by model. Move anything on gpt-5.6-sol to an evaluation of gpt-6.1-sol this month; if quality holds, the switch pays for itself on December 1. Check whether your prompts are structured to benefit from caching, which on 6.1 Sol is a 95% discount on repeated prefixes. And put November 30 and December 1 in the same calendar you use for cloud reservation renewals, because this is what AI pricing now looks like.

item.title: Gemini 4 Argon's launch price ends November 30. Plan for $4 / $20
item.description: Google's pricing page now carries an expiry date on its flagship's introductory rate, and the Flash tiers follow in January. Here is the math for anyone who built on launch pricing.
item.content:encoded:
Google's pricing page now carries an expiry date on its flagship's introductory rate, and the Flash tiers follow in January. Here is the math for anyone who built on launch pricing.

Google's official Gemini API pricing page, checked on November 8, lists Gemini 4 Argon at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens through November 30, 2026, rising to $4 and $20 from December 1. Cached-input pricing doubles on the same schedule, from $0.10 to $0.20. The Flash tiers follow a month later: Gemini 3.8 Flash and 3.6 Flash are $0.75 / $3.75 through December 31 and $1.50 / $7.50 from January 1, 2027.

What this costs you

Take a typical assistant workload: 2,000 input tokens and 400 output tokens per request, 2 million requests a month.

  • At launch pricing: input $8,000 + output $8,000 = $16,000 / month.
  • From December 1: $32,000 / month.

Caching and batch discounts still apply, and the ratio is the same either way: the bill doubles.

How the new rate compares

At $4 / $20, Argon lands at the same list price as Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 and OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol, and remains well below the $10 / $50 of the top tiers (GPT-6 Astra, Claude Fable 5.1). Below it, Anthropic's Sonnet 5.5 at $2 / $10 becomes the cheapest current frontier-class list price once the Argon promotion ends. The full table is on the pricing tracker.

What to do before December 1

  1. Measure, do not assume. Tokenisers differ; cost per completed task on each candidate model is the only number that matters.
  2. Route by difficulty. Most traffic in most products is routine. Keep Argon for the hard cases and send the rest to a Flash-class model; the Flash promotion runs a month longer.
  3. Cache aggressively. Stable prefixes (system prompts, documents) at the cached rate are 5% of input price. Reorder prompts so the stable part comes first.
  4. Check your contract. Committed-use or enterprise pricing may not follow the public schedule. Ask.

The wider pattern

Google is not alone. Anthropic launched Sonnet 5 at an introductory rate that reverted on a fixed date, and OpenAI has used promotional pricing on new tiers. Launch prices are now marketing, not cost; the nightly check of vendor pages that feeds our tracker exists because of exactly this.
